planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring into lean, sharply drained acidic soil in full sun; the dense root system from the famous briar burl takes a season to establish before top growth accelerates.

directions: Tree heath grows far larger than the familiar winter and summer heaths, building a woody, multi-stemmed frame clothed in fine needle-like foliage that eventually resembles a small evergreen tree. In late winter and early spring it covers itself in masses of tiny bell-shaped white flowers with a honeyed fragrance that draws early pollinators. It needs the same lean, acidic, well-drained ground as other heaths but tolerates more heat and drought once its woody root system matures. In regions below its hardiness range, grow it in a large container and give it a sheltered spot out of hard freezes.

planting.note: Scatter seed on disturbed, well-drained soil in fall or very early spring; plants form a basal rosette the first year and bolt into flower the second, then self-sow readily.

directions: Moth mullein sends up slender, mostly unbranched spikes dotted with small five-petaled flowers in pale yellow or white, each centered with a tuft of purple-fuzzed stamens that gives the species its common name. Unlike common mullein, its basal leaves are glossy and nearly hairless rather than felted, making it easy to tell the two apart before bloom. It thrives in poor, disturbed, well-drained soil and needs no feeding or staking, but may need deadheading before seed set if you want to keep it from colonizing nearby beds. Leave a few spent spikes standing through winter for seed-eating birds.

planting.note: Start seed indoors and set out after all danger of frost, or plant rooted cuttings; in frost-free climates it naturalizes as a woody shrub and self-sows freely from dropped seed.

directions: Tree tobacco grows fast into a loose, open shrub with smooth, waxy blue-gray leaves and clusters of slender tubular yellow flowers that hummingbirds visit throughout the warm months. It tolerates poor, rocky, and disturbed soil better than almost any other nicotiana and needs little supplemental water once its deep roots are established. Every part of the plant is toxic if ingested, so keep it away from areas where children or grazing animals roam. Where winters bring hard freezes, grow it as a cut-back perennial or large container specimen instead of a permanent shrub.

planting.note: Set divisions or nursery plants out after last frost into well-drained soil; established clumps spread by trailing stems and can be lifted and divided every few years to renew vigor.

directions: This South African daisy hugs the ground on trailing, slightly woody stems covered in gray-green foliage, making it useful for edging, rock gardens, and spilling over low walls. Purple-pink daisy flowers with darker centers open over a long season, slowing only in the hottest or coldest stretches of the year. It is one of the more cold-tolerant osteospermum species and often survives mild winters where many hybrid selections fail, though it still benefits from a dry mulch in borderline climates. Shear plants back by about a third after the first flush of bloom to keep the mat dense and encourage repeat flowering.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or early fall into well-drained soil; the low, stiff-branched habit knits into a dense mound or spreads wider if given room to sprawl over a wall or bank.

directions: Small-leaved cotoneaster forms a dense, stiffly branched evergreen mound set with tiny glossy dark green leaves that give the species its name. Small white flowers appear along the branches in late spring, followed by bright red berries that persist well into winter and attract birds. It is tougher and more compact than many of its trailing relatives, making it a reliable choice for rock gardens, low banks, and foundation plantings in cold-winter regions. Avoid wet, poorly drained sites, which encourage dieback and fireblight.

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in fall or early spring into deep, well-drained soil with room for a broad rounded crown to develop.

directions: Red horsechestnut is a naturally occurring hybrid between the European horse chestnut and red buckeye, combining the dense rounded crown of the former with flower color from the latter. Upright panicles of pink-to-red blossoms stand above the glossy palmate foliage in late spring, making it a popular flowering street and park tree in temperate climates. It tolerates urban conditions and compacted soil better than straight horse chestnut but still appreciates deep, evenly moist ground while young. Rake up and discard fallen leaves and spiny husks in autumn, since leaf blotch and leaf scorch can build up on fallen debris from year to year.
